title: CWG 2026 Day 8 Medal Table: Where India stand after Lovepreet’s record silver and Seema’s hard-fought bronze
content:
India added two more medals to its tally on Day 8 of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, with weightlifter Lovepreet Singh winning silver and discus thrower Seema Kaliramna securing bronze to take the country's overall haul to 17 medals.The latest additions leave India 10th in the overall medal standings after Thursday's competition, with a total of 3 gold, 10 silver and 4 bronze medals. 
While the country did not add to its gold-medal count, another productive day in weightlifting and athletics strengthened India's position heading into the closing stages of the Games, with several more medal opportunities still to come.
Lovepreet Singh wins silver after record-breaking performance
India's first medal of the day came in the men's +110kg weightlifting competition, where Lovepreet Singh produced the performance of his career to claim the silver medal.
Lovepreet lifted 176kg in the snatch, setting a new Indian national record, before adding 212kg in the clean and jerk, another national record, to finish with a combined total of 388kg.
 India's Lovepreet Singh competes in the men's +110kg Weightlifting Final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, Thursday, July 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Eranga Jayawardena)
The Indian weightlifter missed out on the gold medal by the narrowest of margins, finishing just 1kg behind New Zealand's David Liti, who claimed the Commonwealth title.
The silver medal was India's eighth weightlifting medal of the Glasgow Games, underlining another successful campaign for one of the country's strongest disciplines.
 India's Lovepreet Singh, silver medalist in the men's +110kg Weightlifting Final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, Thursday, July 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Eranga Jayawardena)
Seema Kaliramna battles through difficult final to claim bronze
India's second medal arrived later in the day as Seema Kaliramna secured bronze in the women's discus throw final at the EDF Scotstoun Stadium.
It was far from a straightforward competition for the Indian thrower.
Seema opened the final with a foul before responding with a throw of 57.32 metres in the second round.
She then produced what proved to be the medal-winning effort on her third attempt, throwing 58.65 metres to move into the bronze-medal position.
 India's Seema competes in the women's discus throw final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, Thursday, July 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Alastair Grant)
The remainder of her competition was challenging, with four of her six attempts ending in fouls. However, her third-round mark proved enough to keep her on the podium.
Jamaica's Samantha Hall won gold with a throw of 61.66m, while Canada's Julia Tunks took silver with 60.67m.
The bronze was India's 17th medal overall and the fourth medal won by the athletics contingent at the Games.
 India's Seema, left, and Canada's Julia Tunks celebrate after winning the women's discus throw final at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, Thursday, July 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Alastair Grant)
There was also heartbreak for fellow Indian thrower Nidhi Rani, who narrowly missed out on joining Seema on the podium.
Nidhi steadily improved throughout the competition and reached 57.10m with her third throw but ultimately finished fourth, just outside the medals.
India's medal tally reaches 17
After eight days of competition, India has collected 17 medals, comprising:
- Gold: 3
- Silver: 10
- Bronze: 4
The medal haul has been shared primarily between weightlifting and athletics.
Athletics and para-athletics have contributed eight medals (2 gold, 4 silver and 2 bronze), while weightlifting has also produced eight medals (1 gold, 6 silver and 1 bronze). India's remaining medal has come in para-powerlifting.
The latest results place India 10th in the Commonwealth Games medal standings heading into the final stretch of competition.
 India sits 10th in the 2026 Commonwealth Games medal standings after Day 8 with 17 medals: 3 gold, 10 silver and 4 bronze.
Other Indians narrowly miss the podium
Although India added two medals on Thursday, several other athletes fell just short of podium finishes.
In the women's +86kg weightlifting competition, Martina Devi Maibam finished fifth with a combined lift of 245kg.
In the men's shot put final, Tajinderpal Singh Toor also finished fifth, while compatriot Samardeep Singh Gill placed seventh.
Tejaswin Shankar in historic decathlon medal hunt
India also has a major medal opportunity unfolding in the decathlon, where Tejaswin Shankar has delivered a sensational opening day performance.
He enters Day 2 in second place with 4,339 points, sitting just 14 points behind Olympic champion Damian Warner (4,353 points) after an incredible first day in Glasgow.
Because the decathlon is a gruelling two-day event, his competition is only halfway done. He must now face the final five events on Day 2 to determine the final medal placements, with everything still to play for in one of the most demanding contests in athletics.
More medal opportunities on the horizon
Thursday also proved productive in setting up medal chances for the remaining days of the Games.
India enjoyed a clean sweep in the men's javelin qualification, with Neeraj Chopra, Rohit Yadav and Yash Vir Singh all advancing to the final.
Neeraj led the Indian trio with a throw of 79.61m, followed by Rohit Yadav's 78.37m and Yash Vir Singh's 78.36m, with all three comfortably progressing.
There was further success in the men's triple jump qualifiers as Praveen Chithravel and Selva Prabhu Thirumaran both booked places in the final.
With multiple Indian contenders still in medal contention across athletics and other disciplines, and Tejaswin Shankar poised for a dramatic decathlon finish, India will look to build on its tally of 17 medals and climb further up the standings during the closing days of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

title: European football chiefs identify strong candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino amid FIFA's World Cup sell-off row
content:
Paris Saint-Germain president Nasser Al-Khelaifi has emerged as the leading figure being discussed by senior European football officials as a potential challenger to FIFA president Gianni Infantino, according to multiple reports, as opposition continues to grow over FIFA's controversial proposal to sell stakes in the commercial rights to the World Cup.
The discussions come as European football authorities intensify their resistance to Infantino's plan to establish a new commercial company that would oversee FIFA's competitions while allowing outside investors to acquire a 20% minority, non-controlling stake in the business.
Although Al-Khelaifi has been identified as one of the most influential figures capable of mounting a challenge, his representatives have insisted he has no interest in seeking FIFA's highest office.
European officials begin discussing possible challenger
According to 
Politico, conversations among senior European football officials about identifying a potential challenger to Infantino began during last month's 
FIFA World Cup and have accelerated following the backlash against FIFA's proposed commercial restructuring.
Three senior international football officials, speaking anonymously to 
Politico, said Al-Khelaifi has emerged as a serious candidate ahead of the next FIFA presidential election, scheduled for March 2027.
 PSG President Nasser Al-Khelaifi celebrates after the Champions League semifinal second leg soccer match between Bayern Munich and Paris Saint Germain in Munich, Germany, Wednesday, May 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Martin Meissner)
Infantino has led FIFA since 2016, winning every presidential election unopposed, and announced during FIFA's Congress in Vancouver in April that he intends to seek another four-year term, which would extend his presidency until 2031.
One European Union official closely monitoring FIFA's proposal told 
Politico: "The stars have aligned."
The official added: "Whether he steps up is another thing."
Al-Khelaifi rejects suggestions he wants FIFA presidency
Despite the growing speculation, Al-Khelaifi has publicly dismissed suggestions that he intends to challenge Infantino.
A representative for the Qatari executive told 
Politico:
"Nasser has absolutely no ambition, no intention, no interest in the FIFA role, and he will continue to discreetly support all the institutions of world and European football."
 Nasser Al-Khelaifi EFC President speaks during the 32nd European Football Clubs General Assembly in Rome, Italy, Thursday Oct. 9, 2025. (Fabrizio Corradetti/LaPresse via AP)
Al-Khelaifi currently occupies several of the most influential positions in football administration.
Alongside serving as president of Paris Saint-Germain, he chairs Qatar Sports Investments and beIN Media Group, leads the European Football Clubs organisation, sits on UEFA's Executive Committee and is also a member of the FIFA Council.
His influence within European football increased significantly in 2021 when he helped stabilise the European Clubs Association after the attempted breakaway European Super League project threatened to fracture the continent's football structure.
FIFA's investment proposal sparks growing opposition
The renewed focus on FIFA's leadership follows the governing body's proposal to create FIFA Forward Enterprise, a new commercial subsidiary that would manage the commercial rights to FIFA competitions, including broadcasting, sponsorship, ticketing, licensing and related business operations.
Under the proposal, FIFA would retain majority ownership while offering up to a 20% minority, non-controlling stake in the company to external investors, valuing the business at approximately $20 billion.
 FILE - FIFA President Gianni Infantino follows an international friendly soccer match between Iran and Costa Rica, in Antalya, southern Turkey, Tuesday, March 31, 2026. (AP Photo/Riza Ozel, File)
The investment is expected to raise around $4.2 billion, with FIFA working alongside JPMorgan on the deal. The lead investor is expected to be Thrive Eternal, a fund launched by Thrive Capital founder Josh Kushner, whose brother Jared Kushner is the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump. Needless to say, the involvement of the Kushner family has only intensified scrutiny of FIFA president Gianni Infantino's close relationship with Trump, which has drawn increasing attention in recent months.
To secure support from its 211 member associations, FIFA has coupled the proposal with a substantial increase in development funding.
Associations would become eligible for up to $40 million each if the proposal receives majority approval before the September 19 voting deadline.
Infantino has described the proposal as an effort to achieve the "democratisation of football worldwide", arguing that it would significantly increase financial support for national associations while allowing FIFA to retain control over governance and sporting decisions.
European football bodies remain firmly opposed
The proposal has nevertheless triggered one of the strongest public disagreements between FIFA and European football authorities in recent years.
UEFA has issued multiple statements criticising the plan, describing it as a step that "crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross" and warning that "the soul and governance of football are not assets to trade."
 President Donald Trump and FIFA President Gianni Infantino attend a reception at Trump Tower in New York, Friday, July 17, 2026. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)
The governing body has also convened an emergency meeting involving its 55 national associations to establish a unified response.
Reports have suggested that potential options discussed include a future boycott of the FIFA World Cup should the proposal proceed in its current form.
The Football Association has also expressed concern over what it described as the absence of consultation and transparency before the proposal was announced.
European Football Clubs criticise lack of consultation
The European Football Clubs (EFC), the organisation chaired by Al-Khelaifi, also issued a strongly worded statement criticising FIFA's handling of the proposal.
"European Football Clubs (EFC) notes with serious concern the sudden, unilateral media briefings and announcement by FIFA about a potential new corporate structure for the commercialisation of certain football competitions," the 
statement said.The organisation said it was inappropriate that clubs had learned of the proposal through media reports despite representing more than 850 clubs whose players participate in FIFA competitions.
"As an institution that represents over 850 football clubs – whose member clubs, their players and communities are fundamental participants in football worldwide, not least in FIFA's competitions including all the international club competitions – it would be wholly appropriate for EFC to be fully consulted on a proposal of such magnitude," the statement continued.
"EFC learned about this proposal in the same way as most global football stakeholders – without warning and through the media."
The organisation urged FIFA to undertake broader consultation before moving forward.
"EFC always seeks to work collaboratively and supportively with all stakeholders – FIFA, UEFA and all confederations, national associations, leagues, player and fan associations.
"In that vein, we urge for calm and thorough consultation on all topics affecting the football ecosystem, together with more rigorous and transparent governance processes put in place to protect the game for the long term.
"Only in this way can we build the right institutional frameworks and relationships required to promote the true success, stability and sustainability of football."
Leadership debate intensifies ahead of 2027 election
While Al-Khelaifi has publicly ruled himself out of the race, reporting suggests senior figures within European football have already begun discussing possible alternatives to Infantino as opposition to FIFA's proposed commercial restructuring continues to grow.
With member associations due to vote on the World Cup investment proposal in September and the next FIFA presidential election scheduled for March 2027, the debate over the future governance of world football has become increasingly intertwined with questions about who should lead the sport's governing body in the years ahead.

title: UEFA threatens FIFA World Cup boycott over Gianni Infantino's private investors plan
content:
UEFA has threatened to boycott all FIFA competitions after FIFA president Gianni Infantino proposed selling a stake in the World Cup and other tournaments to private equity investors.
The European football body announced the decision on Thursday after an emergency online meeting with its 55 member associations.
“UEFA and its national associations will not participate in FIFA competitions,” UEFA said after the meeting.
The next FIFA event on the calendar is the Women's Under-20 World Cup, which will be held in Poland from September 5.
Explaining its stand, UEFA said the World Cup should remain under football's control.
“Some things are simply too important to sell,” UEFA said in a statement. “The 
FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”
The emergency meeting came after Infantino offered FIFA's 211 member associations an additional $20 million if they approve his proposal by mid-September.
On Tuesday, Infantino revealed plans to create a new commercial company, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), valued at $20 billion. 
Under the proposal, private investors would own a 20% stake in the company. The main investor would be a New York investment firm founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner.
In a letter to FIFA's 211 member associations, Infantino said approving FFE would increase the basic funding each member receives over the next four years from $10 million to $20 million. He also projected that each member would receive $86 million in FIFA funding through 2038 instead of about $36 million.
UEFA, where Infantino worked for many years and served as general secretary before becoming FIFA president in 2016, criticised the proposal.
“This is not merely a profound failure of leadership, but an abdication of FIFA’s duty as the custodian of world football,” UEFA said.
UEFA warns against private ownershipUEFA also explained why it believes bringing outside investors into FIFA competitions could change football permanently.
“The moment external investors acquire ownership interests in FIFA competitions, football changes forever,” UEFA said. “Commercial return becomes a permanent obligation. Investor expectations become a daily pressure.”
Infantino has defended the proposal, saying private investment would "turbocharge" football development around the world. Many of FIFA's 211 member associations depend heavily on FIFA funding.
According to UEFA, officials from around 40 member associations spoke during Thursday's meeting. Several questioned why FIFA was not using its own multi-billion-dollar reserves to increase development funding instead of bringing in outside investors.
“As a result of today’s discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive,” the European football body said, “unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership.”
Questions over Infantino's futureThe proposal has also raised questions about Infantino's future as FIFA president.
FIFA has set November 18 as the deadline for candidates to enter the 
presidential election, which will take place next March in Rabat, Morocco.
Until recently, Infantino appeared set to be re-elected unopposed for a fourth and final term until 2031.
Infantino is interested in taking a commissioner-like role at FIFA Forward Enterprise after his presidency ends in 2031, football officials were quoted as saying by news agency AP.
